extracted.subtask_description: A short beginner-focused guide to installing Isabelle/HOL and learning basic proof workflows via small examples (Fibonacci) that illustrate apply-style and structured Isar proofs. Covers practical interface features, common tactics (auto, sledgehammer), induction selection, and advice on polishing proofs for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation and launch
rubrics_metrics.description: download everything you need with a single click (just choose your platform); install in minutes according to the instructions; launch, on both Windows and macOS after dismissing the built-in protections against Trojans; you can also launch Isabelle from the UNIX command line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 8GB Raspberry Pi should be enough to get started. Follow platform-specific instructions; on macOS/Windows you may need to dismiss built-in protections when first launching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory declaration must match file name and list imports
rubrics_metrics.description: First we need a theory declaration specifying the theory name (which needs to match the file name) and what it imports, here simply Main, a bare-bones HOL environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the theory header is correct before proofs; incorrect names/imports will break processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide correct definitions and types
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply the definition of the function (e.g. the Fibonacci function), which maps natural numbers to natural numbers (type nat => nat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure type signatures align with intended proofs (types often give convenient properties like F_n ≥ 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use apply-style tactics for exploratory proof development
rubrics_metrics.description: Type in tactics using apply, which is how we can apply a series of tactics one after another to explore proof state and generate subgoals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The side panel displays generated subgoals; apply-style is natural for trial-and-error development and for long/messy sequences that don't fit structured proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate induction rule (use provided *_induct rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right form of induction should conform to the definition (e.g. F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n), and Isabelle provides specific induction rules such as fib.induct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add a reference to the appropriate induction rule in the theory file to get useful subgoals. Try different induction rules if the ordinary induction gives awkward goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use auto for routine subgoals
rubrics_metrics.description: The auto tactic can often finish simple subgoals automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try auto as the obvious next step after induction; it frequently proves straightforward cases immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: When auto fails, use sledgehammer for hints
rubrics_metrics.description: If auto is not sufficient, invoke sledgehammer; it suggests relevant theorems and can insert suggested proof steps via the Apply button.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sledgehammer suggestion (e.g. add_mult_distrib2) either by clicking to insert it or as a hint to improve your auto call by including the suggested theorem as an argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish proofs: name them and replace apply-chains with by where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: After getting a proof to work, give it a name and replace sequences of apply-lines with by and a pair (or list) of comma-separated tactics when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polishing improves readability and maintainability; avoid leaving trivial tidy-up undone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep long or messy tactic sequences in apply-style and terminate with done
rubrics_metrics.description: A long or messy sequence of tactics that does not lend itself to a structured proof is best left in apply form and terminated with done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't force everything into a by-command if the combined tactic would be unreadable; readability matters more than concision in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structured Isar proofs (proof ... qed) for readable induction proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To write an induction in structured form, use the keyword proof; induction or cases automatically generate a structured proof template which inserts into your theory file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Click the faint blue underlining pop-up to insert the template; structured proofs are preferable for clarity when a proof decomposes into multiple named cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish structured proofs by removing redundant cases and consolidating with auto
rubrics_metrics.description: If auto already proves some cases, delete the explicit case proofs and insert a single auto after the final qed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces boilerplate while keeping the structured outline intact; it is part of the polishing step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor readability and maintainability over merely 'it works'
rubrics_metrics.description: As with all forms of code, that it works is not enough: it needs to be readable and maintainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish proofs, name lemmas, prefer structured proofs when helpful, and tidy tactical scripts so others (and future you) can understand them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarize yourself with common proof-assistant notation (e.g., 0/Suc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't be put off by the 0/Suc notation, which is common in proof assistants and best for this type of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the basic constructors and notations of the underlying logic; they often simplify induction and case reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take advantage of interface continuous processing while editing
rubrics_metrics.description: The interface allows you to edit your material willy-nilly, continuously processing it as you type it in; subgoals appear as you work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the live feedback to iteratively develop proofs and inspect subgoals produced by tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult the official documentation and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: After trying examples, read the documentation (e.g., the tutorial Programming and Proving on Isabelle's documentation page or from the Documentation panel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also explore HOL/Examples (Ackermann’s function, Cantor’s theorem) and download original theory files to study polished proofs and learn idioms.
